raw_case_text: A twenty-nine-year-old male presented with a history of fever with chills and rigor for 19 days, evening rise in temperature, which responded to paracetamol. Pulse rate was 90 per minute, blood pressure was 112/78 mm of Hg, and SpO2 was 98% on room air. General examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin of 12.3 gm/dL, and leucocyte counts of 8900/muL with a platelet count of 1.8 lakhs/muL and ESR was 98 mm/hr. Chest X-ray was normal. Urine routine examination was normal. Malarial smears were negative. Ciprofloxacin was given empirically outside for 5 days. Ceftriaxone was started empirically; blood cultures were sent which showed S. typhi growth on the third day with sensitivity to ceftriaxone. The patient didn't respond to sensitive antibiotics till day 7. Meanwhile, the Mantoux test was done which showed a 14 mm induration. We did a CT scan which showed terminal ileal concentric thickening of size 8 mm of length 9 cm. The patient underwent a colonoscopy which showed a normal colon till caecum, but the ileocecal valve showed multiple small superficial ulcers with whitish exudate on both lips. Ileum till 15 cm showed edematous, reddish bluish mucosa, less distensible, circumferential superficial ulcer near to ileocecal valve extending to the length of 3 cm with a few other small superficial ulcers till 30 cm (Fig. 1). Biopsies from the ulcer showed acute inflammation mixed with sheets of histiocyte infiltration (Fig. 2). No distortion of crypt architecture or well-defined epithelioid granuloma was noted. Ziehl Neelsen (ZN) stains did not reveal acid-fast bacilli, and Gene Xpert was negative. Intravenous antibiotics continued, and the patient improved on day 11. Antibiotics were continued for 5 more days. The patient was discharged, repeat colonoscopy was done 6 weeks later which showed normal ileum.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presented with a 19-day history of fever with chills, rigor, and evening temperature spikes.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced fever with chills and rigor for 19 days, characterized by an evening rise in temperature that temporarily responded to paracetamol. Prior to admission, he had received empirical oral ciprofloxacin at an outside facility for 5 days without resolution.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated empirically outside with ciprofloxacin for 5 days during the current illness.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, pulse rate was 90 bpm, blood pressure was 112/78 mmHg, and SpO2 was 98% on room air. General and abdominal examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 8,900/µL, platelet count 1.8 lakhs/µL, and ESR 98 mm/hr. Urine routine examination and chest X-ray were normal. Peripheral smears for malaria were negative. Mantoux tuberculin skin test showed a 14 mm induration.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan demonstrated concentric thickening of the terminal ileum (8 mm wall thickness over a 9 cm length). Colonoscopy revealed a normal colon up to the cecum, multiple small superficial ulcers with whitish exudate on both lips of the ileocecal valve, and edematous, reddish-bluish, less distensible ileal mucosa up to 15 cm with a 3 cm circumferential superficial ulcer near the ileocecal valve and scattered small superficial ulcers up to 30 cm. Ileal ulcer biopsies showed acute inflammation mixed with sheets of histiocytic infiltration, preserved crypt architecture, and no well-defined epithelioid granulomas; Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli and GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Blood culture grew Salmonella typhi on day 3 with demonstrated susceptibility to ceftriaxone.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Typhoid fever with typhoid ileitis (terminal ileal and ileocecal ulceration), confirmed by blood culture growing ceftriaxone-sensitive Salmonella typhi and characteristic histiocytic ileal ulcer histopathology. Intestinal tuberculosis (initially suspected due to prolonged fever, terminal ileal thickening, and a 14 mm Mantoux test) and malaria were ruled out by negative Ziehl-Neelsen staining, negative GeneXpert, absence of caseating granulomas, and negative malarial smears. Although fever did not respond by day 7 of intravenous ceftriaxone, continuation of IV ceftriaxone led to clinical defervescence on day 11, and antibiotics were continued for 5 additional days. The patient was discharged in good condition, and repeat colonoscopy 6 weeks later demonstrated complete mucosal healing with a normal ileum.
